# Ancient_egypt claim verification checklist

> Generated by `npm run verify:report` from `content/`. Do not edit by hand; record results with the commands below and regenerate.

**Progress:** 0 / 626 claims fully verified · 0 verified, 794 unverified, 0 incorrect, 0 unsupported (794 claim–source checks).

## How to verify

1. Open the source URL. Each section below is one source page with every claim that cites it.
2. For each claim, find the sentence on the page that supports it. Numbers must match (rounding like "about" is fine; a different figure is not).
3. Record the result (or fill in the CSV and run `npm run verify:import-csv -- docs/verification/ancient_egypt.csv --by "Your Name"`):
   - **verified**: the page states it. Paste the supporting sentence as the quote.
   - **unsupported**: the page does not say it. Find a better source or change the claim.
   - **incorrect**: the page (or better evidence) contradicts it. The card/question must be revised in a new revision.
4. A level can only be published when every claim it states or teaches is verified against every source it cites. `npm run validate:content` enforces this.

"Pre-check" notes were written while drafting. They point at what to look at closely. They are not verification.

"Fact-check" results come from an automated check against independent sources found by web search (not the cited page, which couldn't be opened). A **corrected** or **disputed** claim was reworded to match those sources; the old wording is shown. They are not verification either: the cited page still has to be checked.

## Mystery of the pyramids solved with stars (ABC Science (Australian Broadcasting Corporation))

- **Source:** `source.abc_spence_pyramid_stars`
- **URL:** https://www.abc.net.au/science/archive/articles/2000/11/17/213140.htm
- **License:** reference_only · **Accessed:** 2026-09-25 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.ancient_egypt.stars_spence_drift_errors`: unverified

> **Claim:** Spence noted that the small orientation errors of earlier and later pyramids track the slow drift of Kochab and Mizar relative to true north.

- **Concept:** Lining up buildings by the stars (`concept.ancient_egypt.stars_building_alignment`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L47 “Stars and Buildings” · `card.ancient_egypt.047.c3` (text): Two stars and a plumb line / In the pyramid age, no star marked the north pole of the sky. In 2000, Cambridge Egyptologist Kate Spence suggested a trick: watch two stars, Kochab and Mizar, circle that empty spot, and wait until a plumb line lines them both up. Then you are looking north. The clincher: the small errors in earlier and later pyramids follow the slow drift of those same two stars.
- **Tested by:**
  - L47 `question.ancient_egypt.047.q2`: What makes Kate Spence’s two-star idea for pyramid alignment convincing? → **Their small errors follow the two stars’ drift**
  - L47 `question.ancient_egypt.047.q3`: Stars could set a building’s direction. What did the rising of Sirius set, back in Level 45? → **New Year’s Day**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Modelling the precession of the two stars matches the pyramids' changing errors and dates the start of the Great Pyramid to about 2480 BC. Sources: https://www.csmonitor.com/2000/1122/p20s1.html, https://www.science.org/content/article/stars-date-egyptian-pyramids

```sh
npm run verify:record -- fact.ancient_egypt.stars_spence_drift_errors source.abc_spence_pyramid_stars --status verified --by "Your Name" --quote "…"
```

### ☐ `fact.ancient_egypt.stars_spence_kochab_mizar`: unverified

> **Claim:** In 2000, Cambridge Egyptologist Kate Spence proposed that pyramid builders found north when a plumb line lined up the stars Kochab and Mizar around the unmarked celestial pole.

- **Concept:** Lining up buildings by the stars (`concept.ancient_egypt.stars_building_alignment`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L47 “Stars and Buildings” · `card.ancient_egypt.047.c3` (text): Two stars and a plumb line / In the pyramid age, no star marked the north pole of the sky. In 2000, Cambridge Egyptologist Kate Spence suggested a trick: watch two stars, Kochab and Mizar, circle that empty spot, and wait until a plumb line lines them both up. Then you are looking north. The clincher: the small errors in earlier and later pyramids follow the slow drift of those same two stars.
- **Tested by:**
  - L47 `question.ancient_egypt.047.q2`: What makes Kate Spence’s two-star idea for pyramid alignment convincing? → **Their small errors follow the two stars’ drift**
  - L47 `question.ancient_egypt.047.q3`: Stars could set a building’s direction. What did the rising of Sirius set, back in Level 45? → **New Year’s Day**

## Finding Out Egyptian Gods' Secret Using Analytical Chemistry: Biomedical Properties of Egyptian Black Makeup Revealed by Amperometry at Single Cells (Analytical Chemistry (American Chemical Society))

- **Source:** `source.acs_egyptian_makeup_study`
- **URL:** https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/ac902348g
- **License:** reference_only · **Accessed:** 2026-09-25 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.ancient_egypt.makeup_lab_study_2010`: unverified

> **Claim:** In a 2010 lab study, French chemists found that lead compounds from Egyptian eye makeup raised nitric oxide output, which helps the immune system fight bacteria, by up to 240 percent in human skin cells.

- **Concept:** Linen and eye paint (`concept.ancient_egypt.daily_linen_eye_paint`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L53 “Linen and Eye Paint” · `card.ancient_egypt.053.c4` (text): What the lab found / In 2010, French chemists tested lead compounds from Egyptian makeup on human skin cells in the lab. The compounds raised the cells’ output of nitric oxide, which helps the immune system fight bacteria, by up to 240 percent. That hints the makeup could have helped against eye infections. It isn’t proof it worked on real eyes, and lead is toxic: today the US FDA warns that lead-containing kohl can cause lead poisoning. / A clue from a lab dish, not a prescription.
- **Tested by:**
  - L53 `question.ancient_egypt.053.q2`: What did the 2010 lab study of Egyptian eye makeup actually show? → **Its lead compounds boosted nitric oxide in lab-grown skin cells**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. ScienceDaily and EurekAlert report the Analytical Chemistry study: lead-based substances boosted nitric oxide production by up to 240 per cent in cultured human skin cells. Sources: https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2010/01/100111112845.htm, https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/687144

### ☐ `fact.ancient_egypt.lost_city_discovery`: unverified

> **Claim:** In 1988, Mark Lehner and AERA found a large settlement about 400 m south of the Sphinx, the base for building the pyramid complexes of Menkaure, Khafre and probably Khufu.

- **Concept:** The Lost City of the pyramid builders (`concept.ancient_egypt.pyramid_workers_town`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L28 “Pyramid Towns” · `card.ancient_egypt.028.c1` (text): Thousands of people built the pyramids. Where did they sleep? / And who cooked dinner? In 1988, a team led by Mark Lehner started finding out, just south of the Sphinx.
  - L28 “Pyramid Towns” · `card.ancient_egypt.028.c2` (text): The Lost City / About 400 m south of the Sphinx, Lehner and AERA found a large settlement: the base for building the pyramid complexes of Menkaure, Khafre and probably Khufu. Laborers, craftsmen, managers and administrators all lived there. It sits by a huge stone wall known in Arabic as Heit el-Ghurab, the “Wall of the Crow.” Archaeologists call it the Lost City of the Pyramids. It was a company town, and the company was the king.
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. NBC News (Live Science): the workers' town is about 400 meters south of the Sphinx and AERA has excavated it for about 25 years; Michigan State's site summary: home to the builders of the pyramids of Khafre and Menkaure. Sources: https://www.nbcnews.com/news/all/how-did-they-feed-10-000-pyramid-builders-flna6C9580357, https://www.maxwell.syr.edu/research/campbell-public-affairs-institute/articles/egyptologist-shares-findings-of-everyday-life-of-the-pyramid-builders-during-phanstiel-lecture

### ☐ `fact.ancient_egypt.builders_conscripted_paid`: unverified

> **Claim:** The pyramid builders were not slaves: they were Egyptians, many called up to serve rotating terms of work for the king under skilled craftsmen, and they were paid for their work.

- **Concept:** Who built the pyramids (`concept.ancient_egypt.pyramid_builders_workers`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L25 “Who Built the Pyramids?” · `card.ancient_egypt.025.c3` (text): What the bones say / Their skeletons show backs and knees worn down by heavy work. They also show broken arms and legs that healed after being splinted, so someone was treating their injuries. The builders were Egyptians, many of them called up to serve rotating terms of work for the king under skilled craftsmen, and they were paid for it. Think national service, not chain gang. / Hard work, rotating crews, and someone to set a broken arm
  - L28 “Pyramid Towns” · `card.ancient_egypt.028.c3` (text): Bunks for a crew / Long buildings called galleries run through the town. Each may have housed a za, a crew of 40 men, while they served their term of compulsory work for the king. That fits Level 25’s picture: crews rotating in, doing their stint, and going home. Think dormitory, not dungeon. / One gallery, one crew of 40
  - L30 “Checkpoint: The Pyramids” · `card.ancient_egypt.030.c4` (text): One story / Crews of Egyptians, called up in turns and paid for their work, dragged stone on sledges over wetted sand, fed by bakeries and silos. They raised a pyramid that stayed the tallest human-made structure for about 3,800 years. Then robbers taught the lesson every pyramid had been advertising, and New Kingdom rulers chose hidden tombs.
- **Tested by:**
  - L28 `question.ancient_egypt.028.q3`: A gallery crew served a term of work for the king. How does that fit what Level 25 found about the builders? → **It shows they were called up in rotating terms, not enslaved**
  - L30 `question.ancient_egypt.030.q4`: Pyramid builders recap: who did the heavy work at Giza? → **Paid Egyptian crews, called up in rotating terms**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. AERA: crews served a term of compulsory labor for the crown; NBC/AP: workers were rotated every three months; Wikipedia's Construction of the Egyptian pyramids: skilled workers worked for a salary or as a form of tax payment. Sources: https://aeraweb.org/, https://www.nbcnews.com/id/wbna34794254, https://www.worldhistory.org/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza/

### ☐ `fact.ancient_egypt.sphinx_khafre_mainstream`: unverified

> **Claim:** Most scholars date the Great Sphinx to the 4th dynasty and credit it to King Khafre, whose face it probably shows.

- **Concept:** The Great Sphinx (`concept.ancient_egypt.great_sphinx_giza`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L27 “The Great Sphinx” · `card.ancient_egypt.027.c3` (text): Whose face? / Most scholars date the Sphinx to the 4th dynasty and credit King Khafre, who built his own pyramid at Giza. The Sphinx was likely part of his funerary complex. Mark Lehner mapped it and the nearby temples stone by stone and concluded that Khafre’s workers began shaping the Sphinx as they built his valley temple. So the face probably shows Khafre himself.
  - L30 “Checkpoint: The Pyramids” · `card.ancient_egypt.030.c2` (timeline): The pyramid age, step by step: From the first dynasties: Flat-topped mastaba tombs; 3rd dynasty: Imhotep designs Djoser’s Step Pyramid; 4th dynasty: Sneferu’s Bent Pyramid: 54, then 43 degrees; 4th dynasty: Khufu’s Great Pyramid, about 146 m tall; 4th dynasty: Khafre’s Sphinx, carved from a quarry block; New Kingdom: Rulers buried in hidden tombs instead
- **Tested by:**
  - L27 `question.ancient_egypt.027.q1`: According to most scholars, which king had the Great Sphinx carved? → **Khafre**
  - L27 `question.ancient_egypt.027.q3`: The Great Sphinx and the Great Pyramid both stand at Giza. When were they made? → **Both in the 4th dynasty, under Khufu and Khafre**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. AERA (Lehner): Khafre created most of the Sphinx; Britannica's Pyramids of Giza entry: likely part of Khafre's funerary complex. Sources: https://aeraweb.org/projects/who-built-the-sphinx/, https://www.britannica.com/topic/Pyramids-of-Giza

> **Claim:** In her will, Naunakhte, a woman of the tomb builders' village of Deir el-Medina, excluded the children who had not cared for or supported her in old age; her property was separate from her husband's.

  - L55 “Women's Rights” · `card.ancient_egypt.055.c3` (text): Naunakhte’s will / Naunakhte lived in Deir el-Medina, the tomb builders’ village you’ll visit in Level 59. ### ☐ `fact.ancient_egypt.flax_linen`: unverified

> **Claim:** Early Egyptian farmers grew flax and wove it into linen.

- **Concept:** Farming by the flood (`concept.ancient_egypt.flood_farming`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L4 “Farming by the Flood” · `card.ancient_egypt.004.c4` (text): What grew in the mud / The main crops were emmer wheat and six-rowed barley, with lentils, beans, onions and flax alongside. Flax mattered more than it looks: Egyptians wove it into linen. When the grain ripened, farmers cut it with sickles, then the river dropped to its lowest before rising again. One flood, one sowing, one harvest. A whole country planted in last summer’s mud.
  - L35 “Mummies” · `card.ancient_egypt.035.c4` (text): The heart stays home / Through a cut in the side, embalmers removed the lungs, stomach, liver and intestines for the canopic jars. But the heart was usually left inside, because Egyptians saw it as the center of knowledge and emotions. The wrappings were linen, woven from flax like the flax farmers grew in Level 4. The whole job took about 70 days, and Herodotus, the Greek historian from Level 2, gave the same figure.
  - L53 “Linen and Eye Paint” · `card.ancient_egypt.053.c2` (text): Dressed in flax / Level 4’s flax crop ended up on people’s backs. Linen, woven from flax, was Egypt’s chief textile; wool was used more rarely, for things like warm cloaks. Men wore a short skirt tied at the waist. Women wore a sheath-like gown that ran from the ankles to just below the breasts. Light cloth for a hot country: the dress code was basically “linen, and not much of it.”

  - L53 `question.ancient_egypt.053.q3`: From Level 4: which crop did Egyptians grow to make their linen clothes? → **Flax**
  - L60 `question.ancient_egypt.060.q5`: Daily life recap: how did Egypt’s cats connect to the crops of Level 4? → **Cats guarded the grain from rodents**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Wikipedia: flax was an important crop used for rope and for linen, the Egyptians' principal material for clothing. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Egyptian_agriculture

### ☐ `fact.ancient_egypt.main_crops`: unverified

> **Claim:** Egypt’s main crops were emmer wheat and six-rowed barley, along with lentils, beans, flax and onions.

- **Appears in:**
  - L4 “Farming by the Flood” · `card.ancient_egypt.004.c4` (text): What grew in the mud / The main crops were emmer wheat and six-rowed barley, with lentils, beans, onions and flax alongside. Flax mattered more than it looks: Egyptians wove it into linen. When the grain ripened, farmers cut it with sickles, then the river dropped to its lowest before rising again.   - L14 “Taxes Paid in Grain” · `card.ancient_egypt.014.c2` (text): Taxes you could eat / Egypt’s economy ran without money. The state collected produce, stored it and handed it out again. Officials took dues in grain, textiles, cattle and labor, and a share of each field’s harvest went to state granaries, which held massive reserves. Remember Level 4’s emmer wheat and barley? That was the tax. Coins arrived only in the mid-first millennium BCE, brought by foreign powers. / No coins: taxes in grain, cattle, cloth and labor
  - L52 “Bread and Beer” · `card.ancient_egypt.052.c2` (text): Same grain, two jobs / Remember the emmer wheat and barley from Level 4? That grain became bread and beer, the staples of the diet. Pest control was the main reason cats were domesticated at all. A storeroom of Level 4’s wheat and barley needed a guard, and the guard purred. Art shows the rest of the story: cats in collars, lurking under chairs, just like yours.

### ☐ `fact.ancient_egypt.three_seasons`: unverified

> **Claim:** The Egyptian year had three seasons of four months each: Akhet, the inundation; Peret, when the land emerged from the flood; and Shemu, when water was low.

- **Concept:** Farming by the flood (`concept.ancient_egypt.flood_farming`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L4 “Farming by the Flood” · `card.ancient_egypt.004.c1` (text): The Egyptian year had three seasons, and every one was about the Nile. / Not spring, summer, autumn and winter. Flood, emergence and low water. Here’s how a farmer’s year ran on the river’s clock.
  - L4 “Farming by the Flood” · `card.ancient_egypt.004.c2` (timeline): Three seasons of four months: Akhet: inundation: The flood covers the fields; Peret: emergence: The land comes out of the water; farmers plow and sow; Shemu: low water: Harvest, then a dry spell until the next flood
  - L45 “The Calendar” · `card.ancient_egypt.045.c2` (timeline): One year: 12 months of 30 days, plus 5: Akhet: Four months of 30 days: the flood; Peret: Four months of 30 days: the land emerges; Shemu: Four months of 30 days: low water; 5 extra days: Added at the end of the year
  - L45 “The Calendar” · `card.ancient_egypt.045.c3` (text): Tidy math, one bright star / Remember Level 4’s three seasons, Akhet, Peret and Shemu, each four months long? That’s 12 months, and every month had exactly 30 days: 360 in all. Five extra days at the end made 365. The New Year was signaled by Sirius, which Egyptians called Sothis. Each year it first rose just before sunrise at about the time the flood began. Egyptians long believed the star caused the flood.
  - L58 “Work and Trades” · `card.ancient_egypt.058.c3` (text): Most people farmed / The jokes hide a plain fact: nearly all Egyptians worked the land and were probably tied to it. In theory all land belonged to the king, though people living on it couldn’t easily be removed, and some land could be bought and sold. So most Egyptians lived by Level 4’s farming year: Akhet’s flood, Peret’s plowing and sowing, Shemu’s harvest. The river set everyone’s work calendar.
- **Tested by:**
  - L4 `question.ancient_egypt.004.q1`: Which season of the Egyptian year was named for the Nile’s flood? → **Akhet**
  - L4 `question.ancient_egypt.004.q2`: Why did Egyptian farmers plow and sow during Peret? → **The land had just come out of the flood, soaked and fertile**
  - L45 `question.ancient_egypt.045.q3`: From Level 4: the calendar’s 12 months were grouped into which three seasons? → **Akhet, Peret and Shemu**
  - L58 `question.ancient_egypt.058.q3`: Nearly all Egyptians worked the land. From Level 4, in which season did they bring in the harvest? → **Shemu**
  - L100 `question.ancient_egypt.100.q1`: An Egyptian farmer watches the last floodwater drain off her fields. What happens next in the farming year? → **Peret begins, and she plows and sows the wet silt**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. The civil calendar had 365 days in three seasons of four 30-day months: Akhet (inundation), Peret (growth) and Shemu (harvest/low water). Sources: https://study.com/academy/lesson/egypts-three-predictable-seasons.html, https://egyptianstreets.com/2022/01/28/a-year-in-three-seasons-ancient-egypts-calendar/

### ☐ `fact.ancient_egypt.hieroglyph_determinative_legs`: unverified

> **Claim:** The house sign, also used for the sound pr, helped write the verb ’to go out’; an added sign of walking legs, a meaning sign called a determinative, marked the difference.

- **Appears in:**

  - L41 “Hieroglyphs” · `card.ancient_egypt.041.c3` (text): Signs that steer the meaning / Some signs carried meaning instead of sound. The sun sign could also mean “day,” or name the sun god Re. Others were helpers called determinatives, added to show what kind of word you were reading. The house sign also spelled the sound pr, and it helped write the verb “to go out.” Add a pair of walking legs, and you knew which word was meant: this one is about moving.
- **Tested by:**

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. The pr house sign doubles as a biliteral phonogram; scribes added walking legs as a determinative to write prj, to go out, and the legs mark words of motion. ### ☐ `fact.ancient_egypt.hawara_robbed_informer`: unverified

- **Appears in:**
  - L29 “Why Pyramids Stopped” · `card.ancient_egypt.029.c3` (text): The maze that failed / Amenemhat III tried to beat the robbers with a maze of passages around his burial. It didn’t work: robbers found their way through and emptied the sarcophagi. When the archaeologist Flinders Petrie worked out their route, he concluded they must have had the plan from an informer. The best lock fails when someone sells the key. / Robbers got in anyway, probably with inside help

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Wikipedia's Hawara article: Petrie found the trapdoors not slid into place and burned coffin remains, showing robbers had got in; History Hit: corridors blocked with portcullises, yet the pyramid was robbed. That’s more than four centuries after Egypt became a Roman province in 30 BCE (remember the end of Level 1’s timeline?). The old script had outlived the pharaohs by a long way.   - L10 “Checkpoint: The Gift of the Nile” · `card.ancient_egypt.010.c3` (text): One story / Monsoon rain in Ethiopia made the Nile flood Egypt every summer, and the flood left black silt on a thin strip of land. ### ☐ `fact.ancient_egypt.stone_blocks_sledges`: unverified

> **Claim:** Egyptians moved heavy stone blocks on wooden sledges.

A wall painting in the tomb of Djehutihotep shows a man on the front of a sledge pouring water onto the sand ahead of it. ### ☐ `fact.ancient_egypt.decline_rulers_sequence`: unverified

> **Claim:** After the New Kingdom, Egypt’s rulers included Libyans, Kushites, Persians, Macedonian Greeks, Romans and later Arabs, with a last spell of native kings from 404 to 343 BCE.

- **Concept:** From pharaohs to foreign rulers (`concept.ancient_egypt.decline_conquest_story`)

  - L90 “Checkpoint: Decline and Conquest” · `card.ancient_egypt.090.c2` (timeline): Egypt under outsiders: About 1177 BCE: Ramesses III beats off the Sea Peoples; 8th century BCE: Kush takes Egypt; the 25th Dynasty rules; 525 BCE: Persia’s Cambyses II conquers Egypt; 332 BCE: Egypt welcomes Alexander the Great; 30 BCE: Egypt becomes a province of Rome; 642 CE: Arab forces enter Alexandria
  - L90 “Checkpoint: Decline and Conquest” · `card.ancient_egypt.090.c3` (text): One story / Egypt beat the Sea Peoples and still came out weaker. It split between kings at Tanis and priests at Thebes, and outsiders stepped in: Kushites who worshipped Amun, a Persian crowned pharaoh, Alexander greeted as son of Amun, Ptolemies carved as pharaohs, Romans who shipped its grain home. Native kings returned only once, and Nectanebo II was the last. Libraries faded slowly and temples closed. The crown kept changing heads; the land kept feeding whoever wore it.

> **Claim:** Champollion showed that hieroglyphs were a mixed system: many signs stood for sounds, and others stood for whole ideas or objects.

- **Concept:** Champollion cracks hieroglyphs (`concept.ancient_egypt.champollion_decipherment`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L93 “Champollion Cracks the Code” · `card.ancient_egypt.093.c3` (text): Too many signs / Champollion tried counting. The hieroglyphic text on the Rosetta Stone uses 1,419 signs, while the Greek version has only 486 words. If every sign were a whole idea, those numbers should be much closer. So many signs had to stand for sounds, mixed with others that stood for whole ideas or objects. Hieroglyphs weren’t picture riddles after all. They were writing down a spoken language. / 1,419 signs for 486 words: too many for pictures alone

### ☐ `fact.ancient_egypt.rosetta_greek_key`: unverified

> **Claim:** Scholars could still read ancient Greek, so the Greek text of the Rosetta Stone gave them a known translation of the Egyptian scripts.

- **Concept:** The Rosetta Stone (`concept.ancient_egypt.rosetta_stone_find`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L92 “The Rosetta Stone” · `card.ancient_egypt.092.c2` (text): One message, three scripts / The stone carries the same decree three times. First in hieroglyphs. Then in demotic, the everyday Egyptian handwriting. Then in ancient Greek, the language of Egypt’s Macedonian Greek rulers. Nobody could read the first two, but scholars could still read Greek. So here was a lost script with a translation stapled on. Picture a menu printed in a language you can’t read, right beside one you can. / Hieroglyphs + demotic + Greek = one message
- **Tested by:**
  - L92 `question.ancient_egypt.092.q1`: Which three scripts are carved on the Rosetta Stone? → **Hieroglyphs, demotic and ancient Greek**
  - L92 `question.ancient_egypt.092.q2`: Why did the Greek text on the Rosetta Stone matter so much to scholars? → **Greek was readable, so it served as a translation**
  - L92 `question.ancient_egypt.092.q3`: From Level 91: why did scholars in 1799 need a stone like this at all? → **No one had read hieroglyphs for over 1,400 years**
  - L100 `question.ancient_egypt.100.q4`: Manetho wrote his history of Egypt in Greek around 300 BCE, and the Rosetta Stone decree also used Greek. Why Greek? → **Egypt was ruled by Macedonian Greek kings**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. The trilingual inscription let scholars use the known Greek translation to work on the Egyptian texts. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decipherment_of_ancient_Egyptian_scripts, https://www.britannica.com/topic/hieroglyph

One job was pressing amulets into lumps of clay to make moulds. Fingerprints left in those moulds show that children as young as ten were working in workshops. And work meant pay the Egyptian way: in a land without coins, workers were often paid in food rations. Their work still carries their fingerprints.
  - L60 “Checkpoint: Daily Life” · `card.ancient_egypt.060.c2` (text): Clues nobody meant to leave / Some evidence was never meant as a record. Worn-down teeth show that Egyptian bread was gritty with sand. Fingerprints in clay moulds show children as young as ten at work in workshops. ### ☐ `fact.ancient_egypt.animal_mummies_empty_third`: unverified

> **Claim:** Scanning hundreds of animal mummies, a University of Manchester team found that around a third contained no animal material at all.

- **Concept:** Animal mummies (`concept.ancient_egypt.animal_mummies_offerings`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L38 “Animal Mummies” · `card.ancient_egypt.038.c4` (text): Not always what it seems / Modern scans hold a surprise. Scanning hundreds of animal mummies, a University of Manchester team found that around a third contained no animal material at all. From the outside, a bundle looked like a bird or a cat. Inside, a third of the time, no animal at all. A good reminder that a mummy’s label isn’t always its contents, and that scans can check without unwrapping.
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. CNN (2015): of about 800 animal mummies scanned by Manchester researchers, a third held no animal remains. Sources: https://www.cnn.com/2015/05/22/africa/ancient-egypt-animal-mummies-empty

### ☐ `fact.ancient_egypt.food_rations_pay`: unverified

> **Claim:** Egypt did not use coins or paper money, so workers and household staff were often paid in food rations.

- **Concept:** Bread and beer (`concept.ancient_egypt.daily_bread_beer`)

  - L54 “Growing Up in Egypt” · `card.ancient_egypt.054.c4` (text): Small hands at work / Children worked from a young age to help support their families. One job was pressing amulets into lumps of clay to make moulds. Fingerprints left in those moulds show that children as young as ten were working in workshops. And work meant pay the Egyptian way: in a land without coins, workers were often paid in food rations. Their work still carries their fingerprints.
  - L58 “Work and Trades” · `card.ancient_egypt.058.c4` (text): Craft and pay / Craftspeople worked alongside the farmers, and Britannica says they raised their techniques, many first borrowed from Asia, to extraordinary levels of perfection. As for the Satire, some Egyptologists doubt “satire” is even the right word, because its pictures of hard labor are so starkly realistic. The joke may have been truer than it was funny.

It’s the first recorded strike in history. When your pay is food, a late payday means a hungry family. / The first recorded strike: late rations, empty stomachs, tools down.

> **Claim:** Ancient Egyptian civilization lasted about 3,000 years, from unification around 3100 to 3000 BCE until Egypt became a province of the Roman Empire in 30 BCE.

- **Appears in:**
  - L1 “Ancient Egypt in One Level” · `card.ancient_egypt.001.c4` (fact): Ancient Egypt lasted about 3,000 years. / Count from the first kings, around 3100 to 3000 BCE, to 30 BCE, when Egypt became a province of Rome. That’s one civilization running for longer than the time between Cleopatra and you. Why it lasted so long is this chapter’s story, and it starts with a river.
  - L1 “Ancient Egypt in One Level” · `card.ancient_egypt.001.c2` (timeline): Three kingdoms, about 3,000 years: About 3100–3000 BCE: Upper and Lower Egypt become one kingdom; About 2686–2160 BCE: Old Kingdom: the age of the great pyramids; About 2055–1650 BCE: Middle Kingdom: Egypt is reunited; About 1550–1069 BCE: New Kingdom: Egypt becomes an empire; 30 BCE: Egypt becomes a province of Rome
  - L2 “The Gift of the Nile” · `card.ancient_egypt.002.c1` (text): Egypt barely gets any rain. So how did it feed a great civilization? / A little over an inch of rain falls on Cairo in a year, and less than that farther south. Yet Egypt fed a dense population and prosperous cities for about 3,000 years. The answer arrived every summer, from somewhere else.
  - L77 “Cleopatra” · `card.ancient_egypt.077.c3` (text): A queen against Rome / She ruled from 51 to 30 BCE. Forced out by her brother Ptolemy XIII, she regained power with Julius Caesar’s help and had a son by him, Caesarion. Later she allied with Mark Antony. In 31 BCE Octavian defeated them at the Battle of Actium, and in 30 BCE she died. Legend says by an asp’s bite; how she really died is uncertain. That same year, Egypt became a Roman province. / Caesar, Antony, Actium, 30 BCE
  - L88 “Rome's Breadbasket” · `card.ancient_egypt.088.c2` (text): The emperor’s own province / In 30 BCE Egypt became a Roman province, but not an ordinary one. Octavian, the future emperor Augustus, treated it as his own private kingdom, as heir to the Ptolemies. A prefect he appointed ran it, and Roman senators were forbidden to visit without the emperor’s permission. Egypt wasn’t just conquered. It was fenced off.
  - L90 “Checkpoint: Decline and Conquest” · `card.ancient_egypt.090.c2` (timeline): Egypt under outsiders: About 1177 BCE: Ramesses III beats off the Sea Peoples; 8th century BCE: Kush takes Egypt; the 25th Dynasty rules; 525 BCE: Persia’s Cambyses II conquers Egypt; 332 BCE: Egypt welcomes Alexander the Great; 30 BCE: Egypt becomes a province of Rome; 642 CE: Arab forces enter Alexandria
  - L91 “Forgetting Hieroglyphs” · `card.ancient_egypt.091.c2` (text): The last hieroglyph / The last known hieroglyphic inscription was carved in 394 CE, at the Temple of Isis at Philae. That’s more than four centuries after Egypt became a Roman province in 30 BCE (remember the end of Level 1’s timeline?). The old script had outlived the pharaohs by a long way. Its final signs are roughly cut but still clear enough to read. There was just no one left to read them.
  - L99 “Egypt's Legacy” · `card.ancient_egypt.099.c1` (text): You use ancient Egypt daily: in your calendar, your alphabet and your paper. / Egypt became a Roman province in 30 BCE, but pieces of it never left. Here are three hiding in plain sight.

### ☐ `fact.ancient_egypt.unification_date`: unverified

> **Claim:** Upper and Lower Egypt became one kingdom around 3100 to 3000 BCE: the Met dates unification to about 3100 BCE, and the Oxford History starts the First Dynasty about 3000 BCE.

- **Concept:** Three thousand years (`concept.ancient_egypt.egypt_span`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L1 “Ancient Egypt in One Level” · `card.ancient_egypt.001.c2` (timeline): Three kingdoms, about 3,000 years: About 3100–3000 BCE: Upper and Lower Egypt become one kingdom; About 2686–2160 BCE: Old Kingdom: the age of the great pyramids; About 2055–1650 BCE: Middle Kingdom: Egypt is reunited; About 1550–1069 BCE: New Kingdom: Egypt becomes an empire; 30 BCE: Egypt becomes a province of Rome
  - L7 “Before the Pharaohs” · `card.ancient_egypt.007.c4` (text): From villages to towns / Over the following centuries, villages grew into towns. The culture of Upper Egypt spread north into Lower Egypt, probably through trade. Boats are among the earliest designs painted on Egyptian pots, which date to about 3500 to 3300 BCE, so the river road was already part of life. By around 3100 to 3000 BCE, the two lands would share not just a way of life but a king.
  - L8 “Narmer and the First Kings” · `card.ancient_egypt.008.c1` (text): Egypt’s first king? Egyptians said Menes. The evidence says it’s complicated. / Somewhere around 3100 to 3000 BCE, Upper and Lower Egypt became one kingdom. Working out exactly how, and by whom, is one of history’s great detective puzzles.
  - L9 “Counting Egyptian Time” · `card.ancient_egypt.009.c4` (fact): Before 664 BCE, Egyptian dates are approximate. / From 664 BCE on, Egyptian dates can be tied exactly to our calendar. Before that, experts’ dates can differ by decades or more. That’s why this chapter keeps saying “about,” and why Level 8 dated unification to around 3100 to 3000 BCE instead of picking a single year.
  - L10 “Checkpoint: The Gift of the Nile” · `card.ancient_egypt.010.c2` (timeline): From villages to one kingdom: About 5000 BCE: Farming villages in the Faiyum; About 4000 BCE: Badarian potters make fine black-topped pots; About 3500–3300 BCE: Boats painted on Egyptian pots; About 3100–3000 BCE: Upper and Lower Egypt become one kingdom; About 2686 BCE: The Old Kingdom begins
  - L15 “Egypt's Army” · `card.ancient_egypt.015.c1` (text): For over a thousand years after unification, Egypt fought without chariots. / Then came the horse, the chariot and a better bow, and in the New Kingdom Egypt became an empire. How did its army change?
  - L41 “Hieroglyphs” · `card.ancient_egypt.041.c4` (text): Which way do I read? / Hieroglyphs usually ran from right to left, but not always. The signs tell you: the way they face shows the reading direction, so the birds and people act as arrows. The system itself appeared in the late predynastic period, just before Egypt’s First Dynasty, as the Two Lands were becoming one kingdom around 3100 to 3000 BCE. Egypt got a king and a script at about the same time.
- **Tested by:**
  - L41 `question.ancient_egypt.041.q3`: Hieroglyphic writing appeared around the time of which Chapter 1 event? → **Upper and Lower Egypt becoming one kingdom**
  - L77 `question.ancient_egypt.077.q3`: Cleopatra died in 30 BCE. From Level 1, what happened to Egypt that same year? → **It became a province of Rome**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Met Heilbrunn keyword page: Early Dynastic Period c.3100-2649 BC, with Egypt unified at the start of Dynasty 1; the Oxford History chronology places Narmer and Dynasty 1 around 3000 BC. Sources: https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/keywords/early-dynastic-period-in-egypt, https://archive.org/stream/TheOxfordHistoryOfAncient/The+Oxford+History+of+Ancient_djvu.txt

  - L49 “Jewelry and Glass” · `card.ancient_egypt.049.c4` (text): Glass arrives late / Glass came much later, in the New Kingdom, about 1500 BCE. It took two stages: first the raw glass was made, then it was reheated and shaped. That means Egyptians were making faience for some 2,500 years before they made glass. Patience, or just very good faience.
- **Tested by:**
  - L49 `question.ancient_egypt.049.q2`: How could Egyptian jewelers get those colors without the real stones? → **By using faience and glassy pastes**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Egyptian faience is a quartz-based ceramic with an alkaline glaze colored by copper; glazed beads appear in predynastic graves. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egyptian_faience, https://blogs.ucl.ac.uk/researchers-in-museums/2017/02/02/question-of-the-week-what-is-egyptian-faience/

If it came too big or too small, they blamed an angry river or a king who had slipped in his duties.
  - L56 “Cats and Other Pets” · `card.ancient_egypt.056.c4` (text): Mourning the family cat / Losing a cat hurt. He called the reigns of Khufu and his son Khafre 106 years of oppression and misery. Yet in Egypt itself, Khufu was remembered after his death as a wise ruler. Whose review would you trust: a visitor two thousand years late, or the people who kept his memory?

A famous writer with a great story still needs checking against the evidence.
  - L98 “Myths About Egypt” · `card.ancient_egypt.098.c2` (text): Myth: slaves built the pyramids / The picture of whipped slaves comes from Herodotus (yes, Level 2’s “gift of the river” man), misreadings of the Bible’s book of Exodus, and Hollywood films. ### ☐ `fact.ancient_egypt.djehutihotep_water_painting`: unverified

> **Claim:** A wall painting in the tomb of Djehutihotep shows a man on the front of a sledge pouring water onto the sand in front of it.

- **Appears in:**
  - L26 “Moving the Stones” · `card.ancient_egypt.026.c3` (text): Water on the sand / On land, blocks rode on wooden sledges. A wall painting in the tomb of Djehutihotep shows a man on the front of a sledge pouring water onto the sand ahead of it. In 2014, University of Amsterdam physicists tested the idea: damp sand is about twice as stiff as dry sand, so it doesn’t pile up in front. The right amount of water halves the pulling force. Try dragging a sled on dry beach sand, then near the waves. / The right amount of water halves the pull
  - L30 “Checkpoint: The Pyramids” · `card.ancient_egypt.030.c4` (text): One story / Crews of Egyptians, called up in turns and paid for their work, dragged stone on sledges over wetted sand, fed by bakeries and silos. - **Tested by:**

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Phys.org and Sci.News reports on the 2014 study describe the same Djehutihotep painting of water poured in front of the sledge. ## Roman Egypt (World History Encyclopedia)

### ☐ `fact.ancient_egypt.rome_breadbasket`: unverified

> **Claim:** Under Rome, Egypt’s granaries became Rome’s property, and Egypt became the breadbasket of the empire.

- **Concept:** Rome’s breadbasket (`concept.ancient_egypt.roman_egypt_grain`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L88 “Rome's Breadbasket” · `card.ancient_egypt.088.c3` (text): Four months of bread / Why the fuss? Grain. Egypt’s granaries now belonged to Rome, and Egypt became the empire’s breadbasket. The historian Josephus, writing in the 1st century CE, said Egypt sent Rome enough grain to feed it for four months of the year, on top of its tax money. Four months out of twelve: a third of the city’s year, from one province. / Egypt fed Rome a third of the year
  - L90 “Checkpoint: Decline and Conquest” · `card.ancient_egypt.090.c3` (text): One story / Egypt beat the Sea Peoples and still came out weaker. It split between kings at Tanis and priests at Thebes, and outsiders stepped in: Kushites who worshipped Amun, a Persian crowned pharaoh, Alexander greeted as son of Amun, Ptolemies carved as pharaohs, Romans who shipped its grain home. Native kings returned only once, and Nectanebo II was the last. Libraries faded slowly and temples closed. The crown kept changing heads; the land kept feeding whoever wore it.
- **Tested by:**
  - L88 `question.ancient_egypt.088.q1`: According to Josephus, for how much of the year did Egyptian grain feed Rome? → **About four months**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. UNRV (How Roman Egypt fed the city of Rome): Egyptian grain shipped from Alexandria was central to feeding Rome. Sources: https://www.unrv.com/articles/how-roman-egypt-fed-the-city-of-rome.php

## The Satire of the Trades (World History Encyclopedia)

- **Source:** `source.whe_satire_trades`
- **URL:** https://www.worldhistory.org/article/1074/the-satire-of-the-trades/
- **License:** reference_only · **Accessed:** 2026-09-25 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.ancient_egypt.satire_trades_dating`: unverified

> **Claim:** The Satire of the Trades probably dates to the Middle Kingdom, and students were still copying it as a writing exercise centuries later, in the New Kingdom.

- **Concept:** Work and trades (`concept.ancient_egypt.daily_work_trades`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L58 “Work and Trades” · `card.ancient_egypt.058.c1` (text): An Egyptian father’s advice: be a scribe, since every other job is miserable. / Egyptologists call it the Satire of the Trades, and New Kingdom students copied it as a writing exercise. It’s a biased guide to Egyptian work, and a very vivid one.
  - L58 “Work and Trades” · `card.ancient_egypt.058.c2` (text): The Satire of the Trades / In this text, a father walks his son to scribal school and mocks every other job on the way. The potter is covered with earth. The barber wears out his arms. The fisherman works among crocodiles. The washerman handles other people’s filth. It probably dates to the Middle Kingdom, and students kept copying it for centuries after. Career counseling, Egyptian style: scare the kid into studying.
- **Tested by:**
  - L58 `question.ancient_egypt.058.q1`: In the Satire of the Trades, which career does the father want for his son? → **Scribe**
  - L58 `question.ancient_egypt.058.q2`: Why is the Satire of the Trades a biased guide to Egyptian jobs? → **It mocks other jobs to persuade a boy to become a scribe**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. The text is believed composed in the Middle Kingdom (12th Dynasty) and was used for centuries by children learning to read. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Satire_of_the_Trades, https://www.labrujulaverde.com/en/2024/10/the-satire-of-the-trades-the-text-used-for-centuries-by-children-in-ancient-egypt-to-learn-to-read/
